list.listitem: Take a thorough environmental history to assess risk. Pay special attention to the condition of current housing and to occupational exposures. Follow state and local regulations (which vary) regarding screening in children. B
Venous blood lead level (BLL) is the best test for diagnosis and is a marker of recent lead exposure. It is useful to assess for continued exposure. C
The CDC has revised the cutoff for elevated blood lead level requiring further action/follow-up to greater than 3.5 ug/dL in children age 1 to 5 years. B
Decreasing exposure to lead is the cornerstone of treatment. B
Chelation therapy is indicated in children with a BLL greater than 45 mcg/dL and in symptomatic adults. Expert consultation is advised before starting treatment. C
Do not induce vomiting or use activated charcoal in patients with acute ingestion. C

background.definition: Lead poisoning is an acquired disorder of the CNS and heme synthesis due to acute or chronic exposure to environmental lead.

list.listitem: A total of 0.7% of the US population has elevated BLLs.
A total of 1.6% of children between the ages of 1 and 5 years has elevated BLLs.
Children most commonly ingest lead by hand-to-mouth behaviors. The peak incidence occurs between the ages 1 and 5 years. Common sources are peeling paint, jewelry, and toys.
Ceramic cookware may be contaminated with lead if manufactured outside of the US.

Recently, corrosion of lead pipes in Flint has been implicated in large scale lead contamination among children, with the incidence increasing up to 4-fold after a change to a more corrosive water supply. This was due to addition of large amounts of chlorine but without the addition of agents that would protect existing lead pipes from corrosion.
Adults are most commonly exposed to occupational lead by chronic inhalation or contact.
Maternal to fetal transmission in utero does occur but has not been accurately quantified.

Caution should be advised for patients taking traditional medicines, particularly Middle Eastern and Chinese traditional medicines that may contain lead. In addition, investigators in 1 study found that one-fifth of both US-manufactured and Indian-manufactured ayurvedic medicines purchased via the Internet contained detectable lead, mercury, or arsenic.
Elevated blood lead levels have been reported from retained bullet fragments.
Lead competes for calcium-binding sites, which results in uptake by nerves and subsequent neuropathy.
Recent evidence links lead exposure to neurodegenerative disease, including Alzheimer's disease.
Lead substitution for zinc results in disordered heme synthesis.
Inhibition of antioxidative enzymes leads to immune suppression.
Sequestration in bone with slow mobilization results in a long half-life of approximately 2 years. The major lead burden on the body is within bone.
Screen immigrant children and siblings of children with lead poisoning. C
CDC guidelines recommend screening according to state or federal guidelines for geographic area, as environmental lead levels vary considerably. C
A systematic review found that the accuracy of lead screening questionnaires varies greatly and that overall they perform little better than chance.
Avoidance of lead exposure is the best prevention.C

The USPSTF concludes that evidence is insufficient to assess the benefits and harms of screening for elevated lead levels in asymptomatic children or in asymptomatic pregnant women. This is not a recommendation against screening, and some federal programs such as Medicaid may require it for young children. B
A study concluded that screening child psychiatric inpatients for elevated BLL is not cost-effective.
Suspect lead toxicity in a child with growth retardation, behavioral or attention disorders, or speech/language dysfunction. C
Venous blood lead level (BLL) is the most accurate diagnostic test. C

The CDC has revised the cutoff for elevated blood lead level requiring further action/follow-up to greater than 3.5 ug/dL in children age 1 to 5 years. See for CDC's recommeded actions based on blood lead levels B
Suspect lead toxicity in a child with growth retardation, behavioral or attention disorders, or speech/language dysfunction.

Ask about the age of housing. Children living in a house built before 1950 have a much higher risk of elevated BLL. For example, in 1 study, living in a house built before 1950 had a sensitivity of 79% for a BLL greater than 20 mcg/dL, with a negative predictive value of 99.6% for a BLL less than or equal to 20 mcg/dL. B
Other symptoms include headache, constipation, abdominal pain, change in appetite, and agitation.
In adults, suspect lead toxicity in patients with known environmental exposure to lead, and hypertension, kidney failure, infertility, CNS dysfunction, or gout.
Physical findings of CNS dysfunction (eg, encephalopathy and peripheral polyneuropathy) or pallor secondary to anemia are rare.

If lead toxicity is suspected, order a BLL. The CDC recommends use of laboratories that can achieve routine performance of +2 mcg/dL for blood lead analysis. A CBC may show microcytic anemia. Peripheral smears may be helpful and show microcytic, hypochromic anemia. Basophilic stippling is a classic finding on the smear.

The CDC has revised the cutoff for elevated blood lead level requiring further action/follow-up to greater than 3.5 ug/dL in children age 1 to 5 years. See for CDC's recommeded actions based on blood lead levels.

Screening is often performed with capillary blood samples. Sensitivity is 100% for a capillary lead level of 8 mcg/dL; the false-positive rate is 20%. As the lead level increases, the sensitivity decreases, as does the false-positive rate.
Venous BLL measures recent lead exposure and is the best test for diagnosis and surveillance. The venous BLL is considered elevated if it is greater than 5 mcg/dL.
Zinc protoporphyrin is not useful for screening.
Free erythrocyte protoporphyrin is not useful for screening and is not specific for lead toxicity.

A clinical decision rule using census block, socioeconomic characteristics, personal demographics and Medicaid status accurately predicted blood lead levels. The rule had excellent sensitivity (99%) but poor specificity (20%).
See algorithm in .
Stop exposure to lead in all persons with an elevated BLL.
BLL <45 mcg/dL: remove environmental and occupational exposures.
BLL =45 to 69 mcg/dL: chelation therapy in children; consider chelation in adults, if symptomatic.
BLL >70 mcg/dL: hospitalization, chelation therapy, and expert consultation.

Chelation therapy may be recommended for children with a BLL of 45 mcg/dL or greater. However, a systematic review commissioned by the USPSTF concluded that the evidence of sustained benefit was limited.
Consider chelation therapy for adults, if symptomatic. There are no evidence-based guidelines for the treatment of adults, and expert consultation is advised before starting chelation therapy.

Succimer is an FDA-approved oral chelating agent that may be used in adults and children. It is the therapy of choice in asymptomatic or mild lead toxicity. Use of succimer in patients with a BLL of less than 45 mcg/dL has not been shown to improve neurodevelopment outcomes in children.

Dimercaprol is an FDA-approved intramuscular chelating agent given several times daily. Use dimercaprol if the patient has encephalopathy or severe symptoms. Do not give to patients with an allergy to peanuts.
Edetate calcium disodium (CaEDTA) is an FDA-approved IV chelating agent. You must give dimercaprol 4 hours prior to starting CaEDTA as it can increase CNS lead levels if given as monotherapy.

Decreasing lead exposure is recommended for both treatment and prevention. This can include lead-based paint stabilization, professional cleaning, and removal or replacement of building components are the most effective and practical measures.

However, a Cochrane review of 14 clinical trials with 2643 children concluded that there is no evidence that lead education or dust control performed by the family have any effect on lead levels.There is also insufficient evidence regarding soil replacement or abatement measures.
There is no evidence that dietary calcium supplementation is effective.
Do not induce vomiting in a patient with acute ingestion.
Consider hospitalization for children with a BLL of greater than 70 mcg/dL, or if the child is unstable. Also consider hospitalization for adults with encephalopathy or renal failure.
Consult a physician experienced in lead toxicity for a hospitalized patient.
All elevated blood levels (BLLs) require follow-up. C
Even a BLL as low as 5 to 9 mcg/dL in children and adults is associated with a statistically significant increased risk of all-cause mortality.
A New Zealand cohort study with 38 year follow-up found that IQ decline by 1.6 points for every m mcg/dL increase in blood lead levels measured at age 11 years.

Higher average lifetime BLLs also correlate with decreased cognitive function. IQ declines an average of 7.4 points for an average lifetime BLL of 10 mcg/dL. Overall, increased average lifetime BLL of 1 mcg/dL decreases IQ 0.46 points.
In addition, a recent review concluded that the neurotoxic effects of lead in workers appear to be initiated at BLL below 18 mcg/dL (10.7-17.5 mcg/dL).
Gestational hypertension and pre-eclampsia are associated with elevated blood lead levels among pregnant women.
Elevated blood levels are associated with worse measures of renal function as well.
Lead levels are associated with conduct problems as well as reduced IQ.

A large retrospective cohort study found an association between blood lead levels > 2 mcg/dl and beahvioral problems in 3rd through 8th graders in North Carolina. This may be confounded by socioeconomic status and other factors, though.

The CDC recommends more frequent blood lead screening (ie, more than annually) for a child whose BLL is approaching 10 mcg/dL, particularly if the child is younger than 2 years, was tested at the start of warm weather when BLLs tend to increase, or is at high risk for lead exposures.

Venous blood lead levels (BLLs) may increase 20% during pregnancy due to mobilization from bone and can be transferred to the fetus. Guidelines for treatment of elevated BLL during pregnancy are not well established.
Lead levels in breast milk are similar to the mother's BLL.
Pregnant women should avoid occupational and environmental lead exposure.

Identify and remove environmental lead exposures, order CBC, and peripheral smear.
Avoid occupational exposures. Stabilize lead-based paint and replace building components.
Chelation therapy for children and symptomatic adults. Strict avoidance of exposures.
Hospitalization for chelation therapy and expert consultation.

feature.caption: Recommended Actions Based on Blood Lead Level

tr.td: Perform routine health maintenance including assessment of nutrition, physical and mental development, and iron deficiency risk factorsRepeat the BLL in 6 to 12 months if the child is at high risk or risk changes during the timeframe

Re-test venous BLL within 1 to 3 months to ensure the lead level is not rising. If it is stable or decreasing, retest the BLL in 3 months. Refer patient to local health authorities if such resources are availableEnsure iron sufficiency with adequate laboratory testing (CBC, Ferritin, CRP) and treatment per AAP guidelines.

Perform steps as described above for levels 3.5 to 14 mcg/dL (0.17 to 0.68 micromol/L). Confirm the BLL with repeat venous sample within 1 to 2 weeks or more rapidly for higher levels.Specific evaluation of the child (eg, a plain abdominal radiograph) should be considered based on the environmental investigation and history (eg, pica for paint chips, mouthing behaviors).Contact local PEHSU or PCC for guidance if considering treatment

Follow guidance for BLL 15 to 44 mcg/dL (0.72 to 2.13 micromol/L) as listed above. Confirm the BLL with repeat venous lead level.Perform chelation therapy (managed with the assistance of an experienced provider).Hospitalize patients in whom lead-safe housing cannot be assured and all patients with BLL >69 mcg/dL
